演奏時吹氣使雙簧與管內空氣振動，手指開閉七個前孔與一個後孔以改變音高。初學要點是: To play, you blow so that the double reed and the air in the tube vibrate, and the fingers open and close seven front holes and one rear hole to change the pitch. The beginner's task is a steady airstream and the basic fingering, then half-holing and lip bends for the semitones. Because the reed is broad and takes a lot of air, it is worth learning circular breathing: you store some air in the cheeks while breathing in, so that the sound goes on. It is often played in pairs, one player taking the melody and the other a drone.

The reed is large in proportion, which gives the sound a plaintive quality and also makes breathing harder work. The range is generally about an octave, and some instruments add a perfect fourth; the eight-hole fingering gives the natural scale, half-holing gives the semitones, and lip bends are available. 都杜克管源自亞美尼亞，為杏木製雙簧氣鳴樂器。其古代起源至少可追溯至第五世紀，亞美: The duduk comes from Armenia and is a double-reed aerophone made of apricot wood. Its ancient origin goes back at least to the fifth century; Armenian musicologists also present evidence for the twelfth century BC, while Western scholars consider it about 1,500 years old. In the time of Tigranes the Great, 95–55 BC, its music was heard in the Armenian royal court. It appears often in medieval Armenian manuscripts. Variants also reached the Caucasus, the Balkans and the Middle East; in 2005 UNESCO proclaimed it a masterpiece of the oral and intangible heritage, and in 2008 it was inscribed on the list.

The reed is a double reed made from one or two pieces of cane, assembled in a duckbill shape and fairly broad. Earlier instruments of this kind were made of bone or a whole piece of cane. Common body lengths are 28, 33 or 40 cm, with seven holes in front and one behind; the source does not say what the other parts are made of.
都杜克管（Duduk，H-S 422.111）是源自亞美尼亞的雙簧氣鳴木管樂器，: The duduk (H-S 422.111) is a double-reed wooden aerophone from Armenia, also called the apricot pipe in Armenian. It has a body of apricot wood and a broad double reed; the player blows to set the reed and the air in the tube vibrating, and often uses circular breathing to hold long notes. It is usually played in pairs, one player taking the melody and the other a drone. It is widespread in the Caucasus, the Balkans and the Middle East, and it also appears in film scores and on international music stages.
